5.4 Swaps (Optional)

This content was generated by AI. It may contain errors and is not investment advice.

All lessons, questions and reference answers on this site were generated by AI and have not been reviewed by a professional. Their correctness is not guaranteed. If you find an error, please report it with the link at the bottom of the page. The content is for learning only and is not investment advice.

This lesson is optional. Later lessons do not depend on it, but swaps are widely used in corporate finance and in banks’ management of assets and liabilities.

Interest rate swaps

Section titled “Interest rate swaps”

A company has borrowed 100 million dollars at a floating rate of SOFR + 1%. SOFR (the Secured Overnight Financing Rate) is the floating reference rate commonly used in dollar markets; since June 2023 it has fully replaced LIBOR. The company worries that rising rates will increase its interest burden, but taking out a new fixed-rate loan would be costly. It can enter an interest rate swap with a bank: for the next 5 years, the company pays the bank interest at a fixed rate of 4% each year, and the bank pays the company interest at SOFR.

The amount on which the interest is computed (here 100 million dollars) is the notional principal. At each settlement, the two sides exchange only the difference between the interest payments. Writing LLL for SOFR, the company’s net rate with the swap is

(L+1%)−L+4%=5%(L + 1\%) - L + 4\% = 5\%(L+1%)−L+4%=5%

The floating-rate loan has become a fixed-rate loan.

Check C1
In an interest rate swap with a notional principal of 100 million dollars, the two sides exchange 100 million dollars at the start and exchange it back at maturity.
If both sides paid each other 100 million dollars in the same currency at the start and again at maturity, what would these payments net to? What does the swap actually exchange?

Pricing swaps

Section titled “Pricing swaps”

For the party paying fixed, a swap is equivalent to two transactions: holding a floating-rate bond with a face value equal to the notional principal (receiving SOFR), and issuing a bond whose coupon is the fixed rate (paying the fixed interest). The floating-rate bond’s interest is reset to the market rate each period, so right after each reset it is worth exactly its face value. Therefore, just after a settlement date, for the party paying fixed:

V=100−BFV = 100 - B_FV=100−BF​

where the notional principal is written as 100 and BFB_FBF​ is the price of the fixed-rate bond discounted at current market rates (3.3 Bond Pricing). A swap can also be seen as a series of forward contracts (5.1 Forwards and Futures), each agreeing to exchange the floating rate for the fixed rate in one period.

At the start, the two sides choose the fixed rate that makes the swap worth 0; this rate is the swap rate. Writing ZtZ_tZt​ for the price of a zero-coupon bond paying 1 dollar in ttt years (3.3 Bond Pricing), the swap rate sss of an nnn-year swap settled once a year satisfies s∑t=1nZt+Zn=1s \sum_{t=1}^{n} Z_t + Z_n = 1s∑t=1n​Zt​+Zn​=1, that is,

s=1−Zn∑t=1nZts = \frac{1 - Z_n}{\sum_{t=1}^{n} Z_t}s=∑t=1n​Zt​1−Zn​​

It is the coupon rate of an nnn-year bond issued at par. After the start, market rates change and the swap is no longer worth 0.

Check C2
A swap was worth 0 when it was signed. Since then, market rates at all maturities have risen. Now:
The party receiving fixed is like someone holding a fixed-rate bond. What happens to the price of a fixed-rate bond when rates rise?
The swap rate makes the value 0 only at signing. After that the fixed side stays the same while the floating side follows market rates; can the value still be 0?

In Figure 2-1, change the years remaining from 2 to 8. At a market rate of 5%, the value to the party paying fixed:
Paying 1 percentage point less interest each year: is that worth the same over 2 years as over 8?

Uses of swaps

Section titled “Uses of swaps”
  • Changing the form of a liability: like the company above, turning a floating-rate liability into a fixed-rate one, or the reverse.
  • Managing interest rate risk: banks, insurers and pension funds use swaps to adjust the duration (modified duration) of their assets or liabilities without buying or selling large amounts of bonds. Entering a swap costs nothing up front, so the adjustment is cheap.
  • Expressing a view on rates: someone who expects rates to rise can pay fixed, and someone who expects them to fall can receive fixed. The swap is then not a hedge but speculation.

A swap is a private contract between two parties. If one side defaults, the other loses whatever value the swap has for it; this is counterparty risk. After the 2008 financial crisis, the US Dodd–Frank Act of 2010 required standardized swaps to be cleared through central clearing houses, with margin, much like futures (5.1 Forwards and Futures).

Swaps are sometimes also promoted as a tool that lowers both sides’ borrowing costs at once; Exercises Question 3 tests this claim.

Check C4
A bank's assets are mainly 30-year fixed-rate mortgages, and its liabilities are mainly deposits whose rates follow the market. To reduce its losses if rates rise, it should:
When rates rise, which side of the bank suffers, its assets or its liabilities? Does a receive-fixed swap gain or lose when rates rise?
A fixed rate makes the cash flows certain, but is the value certain? What happens to the bank's margin when deposit rates rise?

Currency swaps

Section titled “Currency swaps”

A currency swap exchanges the principal and interest in two currencies. For example, a US company issues dollar bonds, but its business is in Europe and needs euros. At the start it can exchange the dollar principal for euros; in between it pays the other side euro interest and receives dollar interest; at maturity it exchanges the euro principal back into dollars. Its liability has in effect become a euro liability, matched to its euro income, reducing exchange-rate risk (2.7 The Open Economy). Unlike an interest rate swap, a currency swap exchanges principal at the start and at maturity. It can also be seen as a series of currency forwards, and its pricing agrees with covered interest parity (covered interest parity).

Credit default swaps

Section titled “Credit default swaps”

A credit default swap (CDS) transfers the default risk of a company or a country from one side to the other. The protection buyer pays the seller a fixed fraction of the notional principal each year, called the CDS spread; if the reference entity defaults, the seller pays the buyer the loss, that is, the face value minus the recovery value of the bond (recovery rate).

For an investor who holds the company’s bonds, a CDS is like insurance on them. But a CDS buyer need not hold the bonds, and the amount of CDS traded can be far larger than the amount of bonds. In 2008 the insurer AIG had sold large amounts of CDS protection referencing mortgage securities; when those securities fell in value, AIG could not post the collateral its counterparties demanded, and the US government had to rescue it to keep its counterparties from suffering losses together.

Check C5
An investor holds no bonds of company X but buys CDS protection with company X as the reference entity. His position is closest to:
He holds no X bonds; what would he have lost if X defaulted? Does this contract offset a risk or create a new one?
Does a bondholder gain or lose if X defaults? Does a CDS buyer gain or lose if X defaults?

Summary

Section titled “Summary”
  • An interest rate swap exchanges fixed interest for floating interest; the notional principal is not exchanged, only the difference in interest.
  • For the party paying fixed, a swap is like holding a floating-rate bond and issuing a fixed-rate bond; the fixed rate at the start (the swap rate) makes its value 0 and equals the coupon rate of a bond issued at par.
  • Swaps are used to change the form of liabilities, adjust duration and express views on rates; privately agreed swaps carry counterparty risk, and standardized swaps must now be centrally cleared.
  • A currency swap exchanges principal and interest in two currencies and can turn a liability into another currency.
  • A credit default swap transfers default risk; the buyer need not hold the bonds, and the seller’s own ability to pay is a risk too.

Exercises

Section titled “Exercises”
Question 1
Three years ago a company took out an 80 million dollar, 5-year floating-rate loan at SOFR + 1% and entered a 5-year interest rate swap with a notional principal of 80 million dollars: paying a fixed 3% a year and receiving SOFR. A settlement date has just passed, the swap has 2 years left, and market rates at all maturities are 5% (annual compounding).
(a) What is the swap worth to the company now (million dollars)?
(b) A director says: "The swap has made the company a lot of money; we should enter a few more pay-fixed swaps and keep profiting from rising rates." Evaluate this statement. If rates had fallen steadily over the 3 years, what would have happened to the swap's value and to the company's total borrowing cost?
Question 2
The 1-, 2- and 3-year spot rates are 3%, 3.5% and 4% (annual compounding).
(a) Find the 3-year swap rate with annual settlement.
(b) An analyst says: "The swap rate should be the average of the three spot rates, 3.5%. A bank that quotes more than that is overcharging customers who pay fixed." Evaluate this statement. If the bank really entered a swap with notional 100 at 3.5% with a customer paying fixed, what would the swap be worth to the customer at signing?
Question 3
Company A has a high credit rating and can borrow for 5 years at a fixed 4.0% or at a floating SOFR + 0.3% (the rate is reset each year at the then SOFR plus the spread). Company B has weaker credit: fixed 6.0%, floating SOFR + 1.0%. A wants a floating-rate liability and B a fixed-rate one. A banker proposes: A borrows fixed, B borrows floating, and they enter a swap in which B pays A a fixed 4.35% a year and A pays B SOFR.
(a) Compared with each company directly borrowing the loan it wants, by how many percentage points a year in total does the banker's plan lower their borrowing costs? Under the plan, what is B's borrowing cost?
(b) The banker says: "The two companies have comparative advantages in borrowing, and the swap saves both of them money for free." Evaluate this statement: is the "fixed rate" B gets as safe as borrowing at a 5-year fixed rate directly? What does the difference between the two spreads reflect?
Question 4
Company Y's 5-year bonds trade at par with a yield of 6.0%; the 5-year Treasury yields 4.0%; the 5-year CDS spread with Y as the reference entity is 1.5% a year.
(a) Buy Y's bonds and buy CDS protection on the same notional. What is the yearly return of this combination, roughly? How much more than Treasuries?
(b) A trader says: "The bond plus CDS has no credit risk, so the extra is a riskless profit. Let's borrow and scale the position up 20 times." Evaluate this statement.
